# gba-emu: rules for every agent

Read PLAN.md before starting. It defines the phases, the shared contracts and who owns which file.
The benchmark lives at `/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-eval`, referred to below as `$GBA_EVAL`.
Use that absolute path; relative paths break inside worktrees.

## Originality (hard rule)
- Write all code yourself. Do not read, copy, or paraphrase any existing emulator:
  `$GBA_EVAL/candidates/` (gba-core), `$GBA_EVAL/third_party/` (Mesen2),
  `$GBA_EVAL/reference/mesen_step.cpp`, or mGBA/NanoBoyAdvance/VBA/etc. from memory or the web.
- Allowed sources: `$GBA_EVAL/spec/gbatek.htm` (GBA, ARM and THUMB chapters only), `$GBA_EVAL/spec/ABI.md`,
  `$GBA_EVAL/spec/gba_bios_stub.h`, the grader's outputs (scores, `.ref.png` vs `.cand.png`),
  and running ROMs from `$GBA_EVAL/corpus/roms/`.
- No per-ROM hacks: never branch on a ROM's hash, title, or game code. Fix the hardware behavior.

## Code readability
- Use clear, descriptive names for functions, variables and types: `destination_register`, `shift_amount`,
  `fn execute_data_processing`. Never cryptic ones like `x`, `t`, `rd2` or `tmp`. Loop indices
  (`i`, `line`) are fine when the meaning is obvious.
- Official gbatek register and field names are allowed (`DISPCNT`, `BG0CNT`, `IE`, `IF`, `CPSR`, `Rd`, `Rn`),
  each with a short plain-English comment where it is defined, e.g. `const DISPCNT: u32 = 0x000; // display control`.
- Every non-obvious function gets a one-line doc comment naming the gbatek section it implements, e.g.
  `/// Barrel shifter for data-processing operand 2 (gbatek: ARM Opcodes: Data Processing (ALU)).`
- Prefer small readable functions over clever one-liners. Split a long `match` arm or a dense bit-twiddling
  expression into a named helper.

## Ownership
- Only edit the files your task owns (see the ownership tables in PLAN.md).
- Shared files (`src/lib.rs`, `src/gba.rs`, `src/bus.rs`, `src/io.rs`, `src/irq.rs`, `src/scheduler.rs`,
  `Cargo.toml`) are changed only by the integrator (the executor session). If you need a contract
  change, say so in your report instead of making it.

## Git
- Remote: https://github.com/Rohan-Jalil/gba-eval-trial-rohan. Never push; the human pushes.
- Author and committer: Rohan Jalil <[REDACTED:email]>. This is set in this repo's git config;
  do not override it.
- Use Conventional Commits: `type(scope): summary`, for example `feat(cpu): add ARM data-processing ops`,
  `fix(ppu): wrap affine BG coordinates`, `test(timer): cascade overflow`, `docs(notes): phase 1 decisions`,
  `chore(results): phase 1 milestone`. Scopes: cpu, arm, thumb, bus, io, irq, ppu, apu, dma, timer,
  keypad, cart, abi, scripts, plan, notes, results.
- Commit after every meaningful step (a working instruction group, a passing test, a merged branch),
  not one large commit per phase.
- Worker agents commit on their own branch. Only the integrator merges into `main` (`git merge --no-ff`).

## Logging
- `NOTES.md`: add an entry for every decision or change of approach (date, what, why), and for every
  phase record which agents ran and on which model. The integrator writes the agent/model rows.
- `TIMELOG.md` belongs to the human. Agents never edit it.
- Milestones: `scripts/grade-full.sh <phase> "<note>"` saves `results/milestones/<phase>/`. Commit that
  folder and `scores.tsv`. All other `results/` output stays ignored.

## Before you report done
1. `cargo test` passes.
2. `cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` succeeds.
3. `scripts/grade-subset.sh target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/gba_emu.wasm <name> <your tests> <smoke set>`.
   Report the per-test scores, and never lower a smoke-set score without saying so.
4. Your work is committed on your branch, and your report lists the commits.

//! PSG sound channels 1-4: tone+sweep, tone, wave, noise (gbatek: GBA Sound Channel 1-4).
//!
//! Phase 4 contract (stub): the mixer in apu/mod.rs routes the PSG registers here, steps the
//! channels with the CPU cycles that elapsed, and reads each channel's current output level.
//! Volume (SOUNDCNT_L), panning and the PSG/FIFO ratio (SOUNDCNT_H) are applied by the mixer.

use crate::io::PlainRegisters;

/// PSG register block: SOUND1CNT_L (0x060) through SOUND4CNT_H (0x07E), then wave RAM 0x090-0x09F.
pub const REGISTERS_START: u32 = 0x060;
pub const REGISTERS_END: u32 = 0x07F;
pub const WAVE_RAM_START: u32 = 0x090;
pub const WAVE_RAM_END: u32 = 0x09F;

pub struct Psg {
    registers: PlainRegisters<0x20>,
    wave_ram: PlainRegisters<0x8>,
}

impl Psg {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Psg { registers: PlainRegisters::new(REGISTERS_START), wave_ram: PlainRegisters::new(WAVE_RAM_START) }
    }

    /// Advance every channel by `cycles` CPU cycles (length, envelope, sweep, frequency timers).
    pub fn step(&mut self, _cycles: u32) {}

    /// Current output of channels 1-4 as signed levels in -15..=15 (envelope or wave volume
    /// applied, 0 when the channel is off). The mixer scales and pans them.
    pub fn channel_outputs(&self) -> [i16; 4] {
        [0; 4]
    }

    /// SOUNDCNT_X bits 0-3: which channels are currently playing.
    pub fn active_channels(&self) -> u8 {
        0
    }

    #[allow(dead_code)] // called by the mixer (Phase 4 fifo-mixer worker)
    /// SOUNDCNT_X master enable cleared: reset the PSG registers (gbatek: SOUNDCNT_X bit 7).
    pub fn power_off(&mut self) {
        self.registers = PlainRegisters::new(REGISTERS_START);
    }

    /// Offsets in 0x060-0x07F or 0x090-0x09F.
    pub fn io_read16(&mut self, offset: u32) -> u16 {
        if offset >= WAVE_RAM_START { self.wave_ram.read(offset) } else { self.registers.read(offset) }
    }

    pub fn io_write16(&mut self, offset: u32, value: u16, mask: u16) {
        if offset >= WAVE_RAM_START {
            self.wave_ram.write(offset, value, mask)
        } else {
            self.registers.write(offset, value, mask)
        }
    }
}

GBA Sound Channel 1 - Tone & Sweep

4000060h - SOUND1CNT_L (NR10) - Channel 1 Sweep register (R/W)

  Bit        Expl.
  0-2   R/W  Number of sweep shift      (n=0-7)
  3     R/W  Sweep Frequency Direction  (0=Increase, 1=Decrease)
  4-6   R/W  Sweep Time; units of 7.8ms (0-7, min=7.8ms, max=54.7ms)
  7-15  -    Not used

Sweep is disabled by setting Sweep Time to zero, if so, the direction bit
should be set.
The change of frequency (NR13,NR14) at each shift is calculated by the
following formula where X(0) is initial freq & X(t-1) is last freq:

  X(t) = X(t-1) +/- X(t-1)/2^n


4000062h - SOUND1CNT_H (NR11, NR12) - Channel 1 Duty/Len/Envelope (R/W)

  Bit        Expl.
  0-5   W    Sound length; units of (64-n)/256s  (0-63)
  6-7   R/W  Wave Pattern Duty                   (0-3, see below)
  8-10  R/W  Envelope Step-Time; units of n/64s  (1-7, 0=No Envelope)
  11    R/W  Envelope Direction                  (0=Decrease, 1=Increase)
  12-15 R/W  Initial Volume of envelope          (1-15, 0=No Sound)

Wave Duty:

  0: 12.5% ( -_______-_______-_______ )
  1: 25%   ( --______--______--______ )
  2: 50%   ( ----____----____----____ ) (normal)
  3: 75%   ( ------__------__------__ )

The Length value is used only if Bit 6 in NR14 is set.

4000064h - SOUND1CNT_X (NR13, NR14) - Channel 1 Frequency/Control (R/W)

  Bit        Expl.
  0-10  W    Frequency; 131072/(2048-n)Hz  (0-2047)
  11-13 -    Not used
  14    R/W  Length Flag  (1=Stop output when length in NR11 expires)
  15    W    Initial      (1=Restart Sound)
  16-31 -    Not used






  
  GBA Sound Channel 2 - Tone

This sound channel works exactly as channel 1, except that it doesn't have a
Tone Envelope/Sweep Register.

4000068h - SOUND2CNT_L (NR21, NR22) - Channel 2 Duty/Length/Envelope (R/W)
400006Ah - Not used
400006Ch - SOUND2CNT_H (NR23, NR24) - Channel 2 Frequency/Control (R/W)
For details, refer to channel 1 description.





  
  GBA Sound Channel 3 - Wave Output

This channel can be used to output digital sound, the length of the sample
buffer (Wave RAM) can be either 32 or 64 digits (4bit samples). This sound
channel can be also used to output normal tones when initializing the Wave RAM
by a square wave. This channel doesn't have a volume envelope register.

4000070h - SOUND3CNT_L (NR30) - Channel 3 Stop/Wave RAM select (R/W)

  Bit        Expl.
  0-4   -    Not used
  5     R/W  Wave RAM Dimension   (0=One bank/32 digits, 1=Two banks/64 digits)
  6     R/W  Wave RAM Bank Number (0-1, see below)
  7     R/W  Sound Channel 3 Off  (0=Stop, 1=Playback)
  8-15  -    Not used

The currently selected Bank Number (Bit 6) will be played back, while
reading/writing to/from wave RAM will address the other (not selected) bank.
When dimension is set to two banks, output will start by replaying the
currently selected bank.

4000072h - SOUND3CNT_H (NR31, NR32) - Channel 3 Length/Volume (R/W)

  Bit        Expl.
  0-7   W    Sound length; units of (256-n)/256s  (0-255)
  8-12  -    Not used.
  13-14 R/W  Sound Volume  (0=Mute/Zero, 1=100%, 2=50%, 3=25%)
  15    R/W  Force Volume  (0=Use above, 1=Force 75% regardless of above)

The Length value is used only if Bit 6 in NR34 is set.

4000074h - SOUND3CNT_X (NR33, NR34) - Channel 3 Frequency/Control (R/W)

  Bit        Expl.
  0-10  W    Sample Rate; 2097152/(2048-n) Hz   (0-2047)
  11-13 -    Not used
  14    R/W  Length Flag  (1=Stop output when length in NR31 expires)
  15    W    Initial      (1=Restart Sound)

content.content:
gameboy and CGB. The following changes have been done:

New Sound Channels
Two new sound channels have been added that may be used to replay 8bit digital
sound. Sample rate and sample data must be supplied by using a Timer and a DMA
channel.

New Control Registers
The SOUNDCNT_H register controls the new DMA channels - as well as mixing with
the four old channels. The SOUNDBIAS register controls the final sound output.

Sound Channel 3 Changes
The length of the Wave RAM is doubled by dividing it into two banks of 32
digits each, either one or both banks may be replayed (one after each other),
for details check NR30 Bit 5-6. Optionally, the sound may be output at 75%
volume, for details check NR32 Bit 7.

Changed Control Registers
NR50 is not supporting Vin signals (that's been an external sound input from
cartridge).

Changed I/O Addresses
The GBAs sound register are located at 04000060-040000AE instead of at
FF10-FF3F as in CGB and monochrome gameboy. However, note that there have been
new blank spaces inserted between some of the separate registers - therefore it
is NOT possible to port CGB software to GBA just by changing the sound base
address.

Accessing I/O Registers
In some cases two of the old 8bit registers are packed into a 16bit register
and may be accessed as such.





  
  GBA Timers

The GBA includes four incrementing 16bit timers.
Timer 0 and 1 can be used to supply the sample rate for DMA sound channel A

All four PSG channels now work. `tonc-snd1` audio went from 0.0 to 0.98. `chip-advance-gameplay` stays at 0.842, but my channels don't affect it: that score comes entirely from the FIFO/mixer work. The final scores below come from the real mixer after merging `main` (b48003c), not from a throwaway merge.

### 1. What I built and the commits
Everything is in `/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-trial/gba-emu/.claude/worktrees/agent-ad48c768da4b9ac2b/src/apu/psg.rs`, on branch `phase4/apu-psg`. The contract signatures are unchanged.

- **Frame sequencer:** runs at 512 Hz (every 32768 cycles). It drives length at 256 Hz, sweep at 128 Hz and envelope at 64 Hz. `step()` cuts the elapsed cycles at sequencer ticks and moves each channel's frequency timer forward with div/mod, so there is no per-cycle loop. Only the noise LFSR loops, once per shift.
- **Channels 1 and 2:** four duty patterns, 64-step length, envelope, and the trigger bit (only when the mask says that byte was really written). Channel 1 also has sweep, including the overflow check when the sound restarts and after each sweep step; going past 2047 switches the channel off.
- **Channel 3:** two 16-byte wave RAM banks. The CPU reads and writes the bank that is not playing. It supports 32 or 64 digits (64 starts with the selected bank), volume 0/100/50/25%, the forced 75% bit, 256-step length, and the stop bit in `SOUND3CNT_L`.
- **Channel 4:** noise LFSR in 7-bit (start 0x40, XOR 0x60) or 15-bit (start 0x4000, XOR 0x6000) mode, using the divider and shift period from gbatek (r=0 treated as 0.5).
- **Outputs:** `channel_outputs()` gives +volume when the signal is high and -volume when low. Wave digits 0..15 are mapped to -15..15 before the volume is applied.
- **Status and power off:** `active_channels()` reports the four "playing" flags. `power_off()` resets everything except wave RAM.
- **Tests:** 5 unit tests covering duty and length stop, envelope, sweep overflow, the wave bank swap, and the 7-bit LFSR repeating after 127 steps.

Commits:
- `76f134e feat(apu): PSG channels 1-4 with frame sequencer`
- `e0f61d9 Merge branch 'main' into phase4/apu-psg` (your request)

`cargo test` passes (121 tests) and the wasm build is clean with no warnings.

### 2. Scores (audio, unless video is noted)
| test | before (silent mixer) | after |
|---|---|---|
| tonc-snd1 | 0.0 | **0.9815** |
| chip-advance-gameplay | 0.0 | 0.8423 |
| aw-arm-alu, aw-thumb-alu, memory, timer-reload, dma-priority | video 1.0 | video 1.0 (no regression) |

On why `chip-advance-gameplay` doesn't depend on the PSG:
- **Same score without my channels:** graded with the old stub `psg.rs` on top of `main`, it still scores 0.8423 (`tonc-snd1` drops to 0).
- **What the game writes:** I logged its sound register writes over the full replay. It writes only four PSG registers, and channel 3 is started at volume 0. Its music comes from the FIFOs, even though the testcase is labelled `psg`.

Any further gain on that test belongs to the mixer/FIFO side.

Two other things I checked:
- **Output level doesn't matter:** halving the PSG level in the mixer left both scores exactly the same.
- **What's left on tonc-snd1:** in the reference, notes start and change at slightly different times than in ours. The first note is about one frame later, and a later note change is about 170 samples later. The reference also looks high-pass filtered. That points to frame or CPU timing and output filtering, not to the channels.

### 3. Unfinished work, guesses and contract changes
- **Guess: silent envelope stops the channel.** If the envelope is volume 0 with direction "decrease", I switch the channel off (on trigger and when that register is written). gbatek only says "0=No Sound".
- **Guess: sweep time 0 waits 8 ticks.** gbatek only says time 0 disables sweep. I count it as 8 sequencer ticks before reloading.
- **Guess: length reload on restart.** When a sound restarts and its length counter has run out, the counter reloads to the full length (64, or 256 for channel 3).
- **Guess: sequencer runs while sound is off.** The frame sequencer starts at step 0 on reset and keeps running when the master enable is off.
- **Simplification: wave RAM.** gbatek describes wave RAM as a rotating shift register. I use a digit pointer instead, so a CPU read during playback returns the bytes in their unrotated positions.
- **Contract changes:** none needed.

### 4. Decisions worth logging in NOTES.md (2026-11-05)
- **PSG timing:** the frame sequencer is the 512 Hz clock, and frequency timers move forward with div/mod per call because HALT can pass thousands of cycles at once.
- **Output sign:** channel outputs are bipolar (±volume). The grader normalises level, so the mixer's PSG gain only matters relative to the FIFOs.
- **chip-advance is FIFO music:** its audio score depends on the FIFO/mixer, not the PSG (checked by grading with the stub and by logging register writes).
- **Remaining tonc-snd1 gap:** note timing and reference filtering, not the channels.

Review round 1 of 2 on phase4/apu-psg: VERDICT merge, ORIGINALITY: concerns, so it comes back to you.
1. [originality] Some behaviour goes beyond gbatek, our only allowed spec, and reads as Game Boy documentation knowledge:
   - the frame-sequencer step layout (length on even steps, sweep on steps 2 and 6, envelope on step 7);
   - sweep time 0 reloading as 8 (psg.rs:213, 229);
   - the second overflow check after the sweep write-back (241);
   - the overflow check at restart (216);
   - "sweep enabled if time or shift non-zero" (215);
   - the channel switching off when `control & 0xF800 == 0` (129).
   For each item, either quote the gbatek line that supports it in a code comment, or replace it with the simplest behaviour gbatek does state: rates only (length 256 Hz, sweep 128 Hz, envelope 64 Hz with even spacing), sweep time 0 = no sweep, and one overflow check per sweep step. A behaviour that remains must be justified by a measured grader result (e.g. tonc-snd1 audio drops without it), and you say so in the comment. Re-grade tonc-snd1 and chip-advance-gameplay after the change and report both, so we can see the cost.
2. [minor] psg.rs:100: latch the envelope step time and direction in `Envelope::restart`.
3. [minor] psg.rs:503 vs 476: use the same `mask & 0xFF00` check for the silent-envelope switch-off on the tone and noise paths.
4. [minor] psg.rs:270: add a one-line comment that wave RAM is a 128-bit shift register in gbatek and this uses a position index.
5. [minor] psg.rs:412: remove the stale `#[allow(dead_code)]`; mod.rs calls power_off now.
6. [minor] One-line `///` doc comments naming the gbatek section on: the advance/output/restart helpers, envelope_step_time, envelope_initial_volume, register, advance_frequency_timers, tick_lengths. Move the noise output into `NoiseChannel::output()`.
7. [minor] Unit tests: length reload on restart after expiry, partial-byte NRx3/NRx4 writes, the wave 75%/50%/25% volumes, power_off keeping wave RAM.
Grade under the flock lock, one run at a time. Commit, then report the commits and scores.

Address this before completing your current task.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

I've fixed all seven review items in one commit; the tonc-snd1 audio score barely moved.

**Commit:** `5da8746 fix(apu): keep PSG behaviour to what gbatek states`, on `phase4/apu-psg` after `76f134e` and `e0f61d9`. It changes only `/var/www/html/test-projects/gba-trial/gba-emu/.claude/worktrees/agent-ad48c768da4b9ac2b/src/apu/psg.rs`. `cargo test` passes (125 tests) and the wasm build has no warnings.

**Scores** (real mixer from main b48003c, one locked grader run at a time):

| test | before review | after review |
|---|---|---|
| tonc-snd1 audio | 0.98150 | 0.98146 |
| chip-advance-gameplay audio | 0.84234 | 0.84234 |
| aw-arm-alu, aw-thumb-alu, memory, timer-reload, dma-priority | video 1.0 | video 1.0 |

So the Game Boy-style behaviour cost almost nothing. chip-advance is unchanged because the game plays its music through the FIFOs, not the PSG.

**1. Originality.** I replaced each flagged behaviour with the simpler one gbatek states:
- **Frame sequencer:** it now only divides 512 Hz down to the gbatek rates: length 256 Hz, sweep 128 Hz, envelope 64 Hz, each evenly spaced. The comment says the phase between them is arbitrary.
- **Sweep time 0:** no sweep at all, citing "Sweep is disabled by setting Sweep Time to zero". The reload-as-8 is gone.
- **Overflow checks:** the restart check, the check after write-back and the shadow frequency are removed. There is now one check per sweep step: a result above 2047 stops the channel. The comment says gbatek doesn't specify this and it comes from your task brief's "overflow disable".
- **"Enabled if time or shift non-zero":** removed.
- **`0xF800` switch-off:** removed. A volume of 0 now just outputs 0 ("0=No Sound"), and the channel's on flag stays set; gbatek says those flags clear only when length runs out.

**One behaviour change you didn't ask for.** A restart now always loads the length from the register, citing "Sound length; units of (64-n)/256s". Before, it reloaded the full length only when the counter had run out, which isn't in gbatek either. The tonc-snd1 figure above already includes this change.

**2–6. Minor items.**
- **2:** `Envelope::restart` now latches the step time and direction.
- **3:** resolved by removing both switch-off paths.
- **4:** comment added saying gbatek describes wave RAM as a 128-bit shift register and this code uses a position index.
- **5:** the stale `#[allow(dead_code)]` is gone.
- **6:** `///` comments naming the gbatek section are on all the helpers you listed, plus a new `sweep_time` helper. The noise output now lives in `NoiseChannel::output()`.

**7. Tests.** New tests cover:
- the length reload on restart after it ran out
- partial-byte NRx3/NRx4 writes (a low-byte write never restarts)
- the wave forced 75%, 50%, 25% and 0 volumes
- `power_off` keeping wave RAM

**For NOTES.md (2026-11-05):** we kept PSG behaviour to what gbatek states and removed the Game Boy-style details the review flagged. Measured cost: tonc-snd1 audio −0.00005, chip-advance unchanged.
